chunks: Expanding the eye. The question: What can you do expand the eye?
To open up a small eye, diagnose first and fix second. Work out which direction is closed.
If the eye is too short, the cause is signal loss, smearing between bits, reflections or noise. If it is too narrow, the cause is timing jitter. Each cause has its own fix.
Imagine a blurry photo. The blur could come from a shaky hand, a smudged lens or the wrong focus. Cleaning the lens does nothing for a shaky hand.
You look at the blur first (is it a smear in one direction? a haze everywhere?) and then pick the cure.
An eye diagram works like that photo: its shape tells you what is wrong before you touch anything.
A diagnostic tree from the eye's signature to the fix. The first row of boxes is what you see; the second is where to apply effort.
Work from top to bottom and re-measure after each change.
Eye height / width: the vertical and horizontal opening of the eye ("What an eye diagram shows").
Inter-symbol interference (ISI): each bit smearing into the bits after it because the channel is slow. Channel loss: signal weakening along the trace or cable.
High frequencies are weakened the most. Equalization: boosting what the channel weakened most, so the signal arrives more even.
Reflection: part of a signal bouncing back where the wire's impedance (how it resists the traveling signal) suddenly changes ("Reflections and why they matter").
A 10 Gb/s signal runs through a lossy board trace. The eye is short and the edges look slow, so the cause is channel loss and ISI, not noise.
One fix is transmitter de-emphasis: send a transition at full strength, then send repeated bits at about two-thirds strength (about -3. 5 decibels).
On an 800 millivolts swing, repeated bits go out at roughly 533 millivolts.
The channel weakens fast transitions more than steady runs, so the two arrive closer in size, and the eye opens.
Other fixes: a receiver equalizer, a shorter or lower-loss trace, and a wire with uniform impedance to cut reflections.
That is the whole idea: find which axis is closed, then use the matching lever.
"First I'd see which direction the eye is closed.
For vertical closure from loss and ISI, I'd add equalization: transmitter de-emphasis, a CTLE and DFE at the receiver, tuned together because over-equalizing closes the eye too.
And I'd fix the channel: shorter or wider traces, lower-loss material, back-drilled vias and controlled impedance for reflections, spacing for crosstalk.
For horizontal closure I'd reduce jitter with a cleaner clock and supply. Raising the swing or lowering the rate are the last resorts."
Quick check. Which equalizer subtracts ISI using decisions on earlier bits?
